sections.text:
We acknowledge that the word of truth often uses these expressions. But we do not say that the freedom of the Spirit is enslaved to the pettiness of those outside the faith. Rather, Scripture adapts its expressions appropriately to each need as the occasion arises.

For “from which” does not always signify matter, as they suppose. Scripture more commonly uses this expression of the highest Cause, as in: “One God, from whom are all things,” and again, “All things are from God.” Yet the word of truth also often uses this expression of material, as when it says: “You shall make the ark from incorruptible wood”; “You shall make the lampstand from pure gold”; “The first man is from the earth, earthy”; and “You were formed from clay as I also was.”

But, as we said, in order to establish a difference of nature, they legislated that this expression belongs to the Father alone. They took the starting point of their rule from non-Christian authors, yet they did not remain consistently subject to those authors. They imposed on the Son the designation of an instrument according to that philosophical system, and on the Spirit the designation of place: they say “in the Spirit” and “through the Son.” But when they apply “from whom” to God they no longer follow those outsiders; instead, as they say, they turn to apostolic usage, as in: “From him you are in Christ Jesus,” and, “All things are from God.”

What, then, follows from this technical system? One nature belongs to the cause, another to the instrument, another to the place. Therefore, they would have it, the Son is alien in nature from the Father, just as an instrument differs from the craftsman; and the Spirit is likewise alien insofar as place or time differs from the nature of instruments and from those who use them.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Basil's point is that scriptural prepositions are flexible and cannot be turned into fixed metaphysical labels.
Biblical citations are translated from the Greek form used in Basil's argument.
